title: What the first party means by necessity properly so called: removal of the power to act otherwise
source_text: XVI. Etenim qui pertendunt omnem proprie dictam necessitatem cum libertate pugnare, per necessitatem proprie dictam eam duntaxat intelligunt per quam agens, non tantum ad agendum determinatur, sed etiam quae tollit ab eo potestatem non agendi, aut aliter agendi, sive quae constituit agentem in eo statu, ut non solum agat certo & infallibiliter, sed etiam revera non possit non agere; idque non tantum in sensu composito, sed etiam in sensu diviso: ac proinde quae facit ut agens, sive dum agit, sive dum est proxime ad agendum paratus, non habeat talem non agendi, sive aliter agendi potestatem, qualis est in sedente, etiam dum sedet, potestas ambulandi, & vicissim in ambulante sedendi potestas, etiam dum ambulat.
pass_a_gloss: For those who contend that all necessity properly so called conflicts with liberty, by necessity properly so called understand only that by which an agent, is not only determined to acting, but also which takes from him the power of not acting, or of acting otherwise, or which places the agent in that state, that he not only acts certainly and infallibly, but also really cannot not act; and that not only in the composed sense, but also in the divided sense: and accordingly which makes that the agent, whether while he acts, or while he is proximately prepared to act, has not such a power of not acting, or of acting otherwise, as is in one sitting, even while he sits, the power of walking, and in turn in one walking the power of sitting, even while he walks.
pass_b_english: Those who insist that every necessity properly so called conflicts with freedom mean by that phrase only a necessity that does more than determine the agent to act. It also removes his power not to act or to act otherwise; it puts him in a condition where he not only acts surely and infallibly but really cannot fail to act, and that not only in the composite sense but in the divided sense too.

Such a necessity would leave the agent, whether he is acting or is on the point of acting, without the kind of power not to act, or to act otherwise, that a seated man has to walk even while he sits, and a walking man has to sit even while he walks.

choices.why: Kept as the technical phrase both Reformed parties use; it marks the necessity that removes the power to act otherwise, as against a necessity of infallibility.
